data.title: Democrats clinch a historic House majority of at least 258 seats — the largest since 1992
data.description:
Democrats clinch a historic House majority of at least 258 seats, the largest since 1992

JILL COLVIN and LISA MASCARO
Updated Sun, November 22, 2026 at 6:07 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Congress

1 of 6
The U.S. Capitol is seen, Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026, in Washington. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats have secured their best general election result in decades, winning at least 258 seats in an election sweep unseen since 1992 that creates not only vast opportunities to govern but also intense pressure to deliver on campaign promises and priorities.

Democrats have gained 44 House seats so far, four more than the 40 they picked up in President Donald Trump's first midterm in 2018.

The 258-seat tally was reached Sunday after Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeated Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina. Four other House races remain outstanding: one each in Minnesota and Tennessee and two in Louisiana that are heading to a December runoff.

Advertisement

Republicans will have at least 173 seats in the minority.

The milestone in the 435-member House sets up divided government, with the Senate also in Democratic hands and with a Republican president in the White House. Emboldened Democrats are preparing a 100-day agenda to address high costs of living while also confronting Trump with a vast oversight agenda for the remainder of his second term in office.

The Democrats' majority will be bigger than any the party has seen in elections since Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 (258) or the election of Barack Obama in 2008 (257), yet not quite the high-water mark of the Franklin D. Roosevelt-era, which saw House Democratic majorities swell past 300.

It presents opportunities and challenges ahead.

"Like, hell yeah, we should feel pressure," said Democratic Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, a former Army Ranger.

"There are people dying in this country and people losing their healthcare, losing their livelihoods, losing their farms, being terrorized from ICE," he said at the Capitol, referring to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. "If you don't feel a sense of urgency and pressure in this job, and a desperation to deliver for folks, then you don't belong under this Capitol dome."

Election rout creates a mandate to govern

The numbers underscore the extraordinary scale of Democratic wins, which spanned from the strongest Republican states to the Midwest and East Coast, as voters, angry over high prices and the Iran war and concerned over corruption, made clear their discontent with Trump.

Taking control of both the House and the Senate come January, the Democrats will carry with them the backing of voters and the expectations to deliver. The Senate Democrats won a 56-seat majority in the 100-member chamber, their biggest advantage in over a decade.

The Democrats, as part of their 100-day agenda, are planning swift votes to reverse the Republicans' Medicaid cuts and restore the Affordable Care Act tax credits the Republicans allowed to expire.

Democrats have vowed to marshal their subpoena powers and launch a flurry of investigations to exert the role of Congress as a check on presidential power. That includes plans to probe how Trump and his family have become wealthier since he returned to office. Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker, has not ruled out trying to impeach Trump for a third time.

"This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen," said progressive leader Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., at the Capitol.

She called the big numbers "a mandate for change."

Rep. Tom Suozzi, a centrist Democrat from New York and an accountant by profession, said the House Democrats should focus 75% of their time on affordability issues and 25% on accountability.

"Everything should be tied back to the people — and how it's affecting the people," he said.

For example, he said, as the Democrats launch investigations into Trump's financial dealings, they should be connecting the dots: "How does that affect people's pocketbooks?"

The White House has issued a warning to Democrats over their planned probes into the administration, going as far as claiming that such investigations — a standard oversight function of Congress — may amount to "blatant criminality."

A new generation of leaders

After House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., struggled to keep the House functioning for the past two years with a narrow 218-214 Republican majority — meaning any few GOP lawmakers could derail the agenda — the Democrats will have a wide margin that provides the new leadership much more room to maneuver.

Jeffries, who is poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House if his colleagues elect him to the job on Jan. 3, 2027, will be able to lose dozens of Democrats on any given vote and still have the 218 needed for passage, in the face of GOP opposition.

"We're not a monolith — people come to the caucus with different ideas — it's OK," said Rep. Troy Carter, D-La., who is expected to lead the Congressional Black Caucus.

Republicans saw their number of House seats fall to one of the lowest tallies in decades. They're far from the end of the Obama administration, when the House Republicans won 247 seats in the 2014 election and the rise of Newt Gingrich when they won 230 seats in 1994.

Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio, who was elected by his colleagues to be the Republican leader in the minority, vowed to fight their way back to power.

"Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families," Jordan said.

The GOP's highwater marks include the 1920 election, with 301 seats for House Republicans.

data.title: Trump sees difficulties ahead if Schumer leads Senate
data.description:
Trump sees difficulties ahead if Schumer leads Senate

By Katharine Jackson and Ross Kerber
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 3:41 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Katharine Jackson and Ross Kerber

WASHINGTON/BOSTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that it would be difficult ‌for him to work with Senator Chuck Schumer if the ‌Democrat is elected Senate majority leader.

"It is going to be very hard for me ​to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "He failed badly as 'Leader' once before, one of the worst [in] history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again."

Advertisement

Schumer, a ‌New York Democrat, is currently ⁠minority leader in the Senate but Democrats next year will take control of both chambers of Congress after ⁠sweeping wins in midterm elections earlier this month.

Despite the midterm wins, Schumer faces dissatisfied progressives who say a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers needs new leadership.

Maryland ​Senator Chris ​Van Hollen is making a bid for ​the Senate leadership, although Schumer has said ‌he has the votes to continue as leader. A closed-door, secret-ballot vote is scheduled for next month.

After the elections, Trump appointed hardline loyalist Stephen Miller to run the White House, suggesting the president will take an even more confrontational approach in his last two years in office. But ‌Trump also has hinted he might work ​with Democrats on issues such as healthcare.

Speaking ​on CNN on Sunday, Senator-elect ​Peggy Flanagan, a Minnesota Democrat, said she supported expanding ‌Medicare to cover all Americans. "If we ​have to call ​it TrumpCare in order to get it across the finish line, that's fine by me," she said.

Flanagan said she would support Van ​Hollen for majority ‌leader. "What we heard from voters is that they were pushing back ​against the status quo," Flanagan said.

(Reporting by Katharine Jackson; Editing ​by Sergio Non and Susan Fenton)

data.title: World's longest climate summit ends without a deal after fossil fuel dispute
data.description:
1. Climate

Cop31 ends with no deal as longest climate summit ever collapses into disarray

Countries fail to reach agreement on text, which omitted mentions of fossil fuels, after hours of negotiations in Turkey

Stuti Mishra & Nicole Wootton-Cane
Sunday 22 November 2026 15:56 GMT
  • Bookmark
  • Comments
    Go to comments

Bookmark popover

Removed from bookmarks

Become an Independent member to bookmark this article

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Join today

Already a member? Log in

The Cop31 climate summit in Turkey descended into disarray and disappointment after countries were unable to reach consensus on a deal that failed to mention fossil fuels.

Nations rejected the agreement at a fraught closing session in Antalya on Sunday, almost two days after the summit was due to finish in what stretched to become the longest Cop in history.

The European Union, the UK and small island states such as Tuvalu refused to accept the text over the absence of fossil fuels, blasting the omissions as “greenwashing” and accusing oil states of “hijacking” the talks.

Ireland’s minister for climate Darragh O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, called the text “unconscionable” and said its ambition went “nowhere near the level of action that's required to deal with climate change”. A spokesperson for the British delegation said it was “profoundly disappointed” by the proposed deal.

Some nations indicated a willingness to continue working, but at the closing plenary summit president ⁠Murat ​Kurum said ⁠there would be no new ⁠draft of the ​deal.

Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to attend the summit, where he made an impassioned speech promising to usher in a “new era of British leadership" on climate change.

But the prime minister said nothing on Sunday as hopes of a deal evaporated and delegates eventually left empty handed.

UK energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh later called the failure to reach a deal “immensely disappointing” but said there had been “genuine progress” during the conference.

“This Cop sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it,” she said in a statement. “The moment required bold ambition and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.”

The failed deal had acknowledged the planet's projected temperature overshoot for the first time and called for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse it.

It was already heavily criticised by small islands and civil society groups who called it a “betrayal” and criticised its reliance on carbon capture schemes, which had been pushed by oil states including Saudi Arabia.

"It seems like we are negotiating with the Saudis," Maina Talia, Tuvalu's climate minister, commented during the conference.

A representative for the Saudi delegation, which supported the deal's mention of carbon removal, told the summit he was surprised at the ‌resistance to technology, which he said offered a “concrete solution”.

Developing countries had also criticised the deal for not providing sufficient new funds to ​help them adapt to a warming planet.

China and India said they had objections but chose to accept the cover text to move things forward.

Earlier, Mr Kurum, defended the text and said the presidencies had “listened to everyone” and tried to bring the groups together, but admitted there was “no consensus”.

Australia's Cop31 president of negotiations, Chris Bowen, called the outcome "very disappointing" and said disagreements over fuels ​and ⁠climate finance were the dealbreakers.

The conference became the longest COP ever on Sunday afternoon, passing COP25 in Madrid in 2019, which ran 44 hours over its schedule.

Delegates pored over several drafts with language that tried to bridge the position of countries most exposed to climate impacts and those whose economies depend on producing or consuming fossil fuels, but the split came down to whether the text should refer to oil, gas and coal at all.

The first time the transition away from fossil fuels found a mention in a UN climate agreement was at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023. It had been hoped that a series of climate disasters in the lead up to this year’s conference would help to sharpen minds and reaffirm commitments.

The last time UN climate talks failed to get a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009.

Chief executive of environmental charity Friends of the Earth Asad Rehman said the deal in its current form “is no deal at all” and urged governments to pledge more than “wooly” promises.

He warned leaders the “clock is ticking” and said governments must “come back to the negotiating table ready to deliver”.

United Nationals general secretary Antonio Guterres also said he was "deeply disappointed” by the conference’s failure to reach a consensus.

“I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands,” he said. "There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science."

Some campaigners also turned on the EU, which rejected the text while some lauded the resistance shown at the plenary.

"The EU is trying to shift blame onto others and it is deeply hypocritical. At the beginning of COP31, it signalled it was prepared to drop the renewables ask from the electrification target and it has failed to put forward an EU fossil fuel transition roadmap," said Laurie van der Burg of Oil Change International.

The failure is a blow to efforts to ratchet up international ‌action, but does not erase the obligations agreed by previous ‌summits or remove existing agreements on action against climate change.

data.title: Schumer's big Senate victory hasn't silenced Democrats who want him replaced
data.description:
Schumer led Democrats to big Senate win. Now, some say they need a new leader

By Nolan D. McCaskill
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 11:05 AM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Nolan D. McCaskill

WASHINGTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) - Chuck Schumer led Senate Democrats through November's midterm elections that gave them a decisive 56-seat majority. Progressives responded with a collective "thank you, next," arguing he should now make way for a successor.

Critics say Schumer's decades in Washington, his age and his close ties to the ‌party establishment make him ill-suited to lead a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers.

Advertisement

"We write first to thank you," leaders of the populist Working Families Party, ‌which backs like-minded Democratic candidates in elections, said in a November 13 letter to Schumer that called for a generational leadership change.

"If you step aside at the height of a victory you helped secure, you would show voters ​that the Democratic Party heeded their call for change. The new majority can begin its work united and focused on fighting for the people who elected them."

The top Democrat in the Senate for the past decade, Schumer, who turns 76 on Monday, has projected confidence that his colleagues will choose to keep him as their leader in a secret vote on December 1.

"I will be elected majority leader," Schumer, who is strongly favored to win, told reporters matter-of-factly last week.

But in the first contested Senate Democratic leadership race since 1994, the New York senator faces a challenge from ‌Senator Chris Van Hollen, 67. While only modestly younger than Schumer, ⁠the Maryland lawmaker and his progressive allies outside the Capitol have cast him as an agent of change.

Van Hollen has said the 2026 results show voters are demanding the party break with the status quo and adopt a bolder approach that gives new voices, including incoming progressive lawmakers, more ⁠influence in the caucus.

'TIME FOR NEW IDEAS'

The Maryland Democrat has run an increasingly public campaign, though the outcome will be determined in private by 56 Senate Democrats. At least 16 Democrats have publicly committed to backing Schumer, while only six have said they will vote for Van Hollen.

"I'm in this to win it," Van Hollen said on Thursday. "That's my goal. I think if we want to move forward on an ambitious ​agenda ​like this, we need new leadership. We need to change the culture of the Democratic caucus. People need ​to have more input. Our new members need to be at ‌the table."

Democrats flipped nine Senate seats in November, including in several states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of the incoming freshmen said during their campaigns that they would oppose Schumer for Democratic leader.

"Do I like Chuck Schumer?" asked Senator-elect Troy Jackson of Maine. "He's been great, but I do think it's time for new ideas."

In an interview last week on CNN's "State of the Union," Van Hollen cited a "hunger for change" among Senate Democrats and said two incoming senators won despite Schumer's efforts to back their primary opponents. He criticized Schumer for aligning with powerful pro-Israel and cryptocurrency interests in those races.

PROGRESSIVES BACK VAN HOLLEN

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said Van Hollen stands out because he understands how Washington and the Senate work as a past ‌chair of House and Senate Democrats' respective campaign arms, and he's willing to take risks.

"Those two things ​are what we need right now, and we need to rethink the way we legislate," he said, pointing to ​Van Hollen's trips to advocate for a wrongly deported migrant and to draw ​attention to Israel's war in Gaza as examples of his willingness to take risks.

Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia suggested the leadership fight reflected a healthy ‌discussion within the caucus about its future direction. "And there's nothing wrong with ​that," he told Reuters.

Senate Democratic leader is the ​only unresolved role among Congress' top four positions. House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress, where John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans and Representative Jim Jordan will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican.

SCHUMER COULD FACE PRIMARY CHALLENGER IN 2028

Schumer is up for reelection in 2028, ​and losing the leadership race could make him a more vulnerable ‌target, as ambitious Democrats such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez consider running for his seat. A memo from Ocasio-Cortez's campaign acknowledged she could run for president, Senate or reelection to ​the House in 2028.

For his part, Schumer has swatted down questions about his future beyond the leadership election.

"I'm focused on 2027 and delivering for the American ​people," he said on Wednesday.

(Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Cynthia Osterman)

data.title: Washington governor calls for ICE to be abolished after arrests at Seattle airport
data.description:
‘ICE is completely and totally out of control’: Gov. Ferguson speaks out against Sea-Tac ICE arrest

Heather Bosch
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 8:01 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

On the eve of one of the busiest holiday travel weeks of the year, ICE agents arrested two people at SeaTac Airport Saturday.

The arrests, captured in a now viral video, are raising eyebrows and concerns.

In the video, provided to KIRO 7 by iceout.org, masked men can be see surrounding a man and woman on the floor of the jet bridge, where passengers had walked down to board Alaska Flight 1306 to Los Angeles.

Advertisement

As the chaotic scene unfolds, passengers can be heard asking the agents to identify themselves. They don't appear to do so. The woman on the ground says her name is Sophia, shouting "We have a work permit!"

The Port of Seattle said the agents took the two down to the tarmac, where they were put in a car and driven away.

In a post on X, US Customs and Immigration Enforcement confirmed it arrested Sophia Hernandez Mejioa and Ricardo Larrando Mendoza, because they overstayed their visas from Mexico. They added Hernandez Mejioa will be charged with assaulting a federal officer, for allegedly throwing a cup of coffee at one.

"Look, ICE is completely and totally out of control. And today, we are confronted with yet more evidence of this," Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said at a news conference. "The culture of ICE is bankrupt. It lacks morals. It lacks any decency. It is un-American. It is deeply, deeply un- American. And it must be abolished and replaced with something that is more sane."

Gov. Ferguson called on airlines to demand that ICE be barred from airports. In a statement, Alaska Airlines indicated it was not told about the ICE enforcement action ahead of time.

Both the Governor and Port of Seattle Commissioner Hamdi Mohamed, who was also at the news conference, said they'd been working to determine if the ICE agents broke any laws.

"The reality is that federal agents do have access throughout the airport, using their federal badges," Mohamed added. "That does give them access that is very different from even employees at the airport."

She confirmed to KIRO 7's Heather Bosch that the Port is not warned ahead of time about ICE enforcement at the airport, though Mohamed says she has requested that.

data.title: ICE officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying fight
data.description:
Immigration officers make arrests at Seattle airport in 'distressing' scene, delaying flight

CHRISTOPHER WEBER
Updated Sat, November 21, 2026 at 11:40 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Masked immigration officers detained two people on a crowded airport jet bridge in Seattle as people were boarding Saturday, causing what the airline called a "distressing" scene for passengers and employees and delaying the Los Angeles-bound flight.

Video of the incident showed officers dragging away at least one person at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport as a woman screams that her daughter is being taken and she has a work permit.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement said in a statement that its officers conducted a targeted enforcement operation to arrest Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, an immigrant from Mexico who "overstayed his visa in violation of our nation's laws."

Advertisement

During the confrontation, another passenger "hurled hot coffee on the officers," the ICE statement said. That woman, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, was determined to be in the U.S. illegally from Mexico and to have also overstayed her visa, ICE said. She could be charged with assaulting a federal officer.

Online flight data showed that Alaska flight 1306, which had been scheduled to depart at 8:10 a.m., was delayed.

Alaska Airlines said ICE officers gave no advance notice of the enforcement action, which occurred during a busy travel weekend ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

"We are concerned by this morning's law enforcement action during the boarding of Alaska Flight 1306," the airline said. "We recognize how distressing this incident has been for affected employees and guests."

It added that the airline is committed to "treating every guest with dignity and respect."

The arresting officers wore unmarked jackets and khaki pants. The video showed them struggling with someone on the ground as passengers surrounded by rolling suitcases look on.

ICE has stepped up arrests at airports since the summer, especially targeting people who overstayed visas in the past.

Alaska Airlines said it was working with the Port of Seattle, which manages the airport, to see if protocols were followed, and also that it has raised concerns "directly with the appropriate authorities."

The Port of Seattle said in a statement that the arrest was distressing not only for the affected family but for other passengers, and that local authorities would "engage federal officials to understand more about what occurred."

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson, a Democrat, said ICE's tactics were "deeply un-American" and called for the agency's abolition.

"The video is horrific and it is chilling," Ferguson said at an afternoon news conference with labor leaders and local elected officials. "We need a system of immigration enforcement and border security that is effective, ethical and humane. And ICE is not it. It is beyond reform."

Ferguson also said he was looking into how ICE agents accessed the jet bridge and he believes they violated a state law he signed in March limiting facial coverings on law enforcement officers.

April Sims, president of the Washington State Labor Council, AFL-CIO, representing over 600,000 workers, said union members were aboard the flight. She said the action disrupted travel during one of the busiest times and only days after flights were grounded nationwide due to a communications problem. "Airport workers are already managing extraordinary stress, passengers are already anxious and instead of restoring calm and confidence, federal agents introduced more fear and more chaos," she said.

data.title: Trump says he would work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates
data.description:
MoneyWatch

Trump vows to work with Democrats to cap credit card interest rates

November 21, 2026 / 1:27 PM EST / CBS/AP

Add CBS News on Google

President Trump said he would work with the incoming Democratic Congress to cap credit card interest rates, hoping to fulfill a promise he made on the 2024 campaign trail but couldn't deliver on because of industry pressure and a lack of interest from his fellow Republicans.

"I would do it. These credit card companies have made a lot," Trump told Fox News Channel's "Saturday in America."

Democrats and the Republican president have both backed capping credit card interest rates, with the standard proposal being capping rates at 10%. It would substantially reduce what credit card companies can charge customers. The median credit card interest rate is roughly 22.2%, according to an August survey by the New York Federal Reserve. 

With rates at 10%, a cardholder with a $5,000 balance would pay about $42 per month in interest. At the current average rate of 22%, they would owe about $100 per month. 

Mr. Trump proposed capping credit card interest rates in January, as part of the White House's affordability push. Banks and credit card companies immediately and aggressively opposed the proposal, saying any interest rate cap would force them to cancel cards for the poor and less creditworthy customers or substantially cut back on the rewards they offer when customers spend on their cards.

The proposal also did not sit well with Republicans, and there was little effort by the GOP-controlled Congress to fulfill Mr. Trump's promise.

That could change now that Democrats will control both the House and Senate. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who is expected to be the next chair of the Senate Banking Committee, has said repeatedly she wants to cap rates. 

In response to the Fox News interview, Warren said: "Let's cap credit card interest rates and save Americans money." Warren told CBS News in January 2026 that she believes Congress could work with Mr. Trump to cap rates. 

Researchers who studied Mr. Trump's campaign pledge after it was first announced found that Americans would save roughly $100 billion in interest a year if credit card rates were capped at 10%. The same researchers found that while the credit card industry would take a major hit, it would still be profitable, although credit card rewards and other perks might be scaled back.

About 195 million people in the United States had credit cards in 2024 and were assessed $160 billion in interest charges, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau says.

Americans are now carrying more credit card debt than ever, to the tune of about $1.23 trillion, according to figures from the New York Federal Reserve for the third quarter last year.

data.title: Abdul El-Sayed catches Trump's attention with pitch for 'Trumpcare'
data.description:
Donald Trump

Abdul El-Sayed catches Trump’s attention with pitch for ‘Trumpcare’

El-Sayed, a former public health official who made Medicare for All a cornerstone of his campaign, included mock images of “Trumpcare” cards in the post.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Nov. 21, 2026, 7:37 PM EST
By Kyla Guilfoil

President Donald Trump responded on Saturday to Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s push for universal healthcare after the progressive Michigan Democrat pitched that it be called “Trumpcare.”

“Donald, this is on the table,” El-Sayed wrote in a post on X last week. “Guarantee healthcare for every American, from cradle to grave.”

El-Sayed, a former public health official who made Medicare for All a cornerstone of his campaign, included mock images of “Trumpcare” cards in the post. The cards are branded with the title named after the president and are golden, an homage to Trump’s favorite color.

Trump reposted a screenshot of El-Sayed’s post on Truth Social Saturday, though he didn’t include any text with it.

However, he said in a phone interview with Fox News earlier in the day that he believes the government could “do tremendous things on healthcare” after Democrats take control of Congress in January.

“They have some good points on healthcare, and they have some bad points, and we have some good things, and probably they would say we have some bad things,” Trump said, referring to congressional Democrats. “But there’s a chance we could get great healthcare and a lot of other things, and we do it in a bipartisan way.”

Trump also told reporters at a press conference Friday that he is “open to great healthcare.”

“There’s a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on healthcare,” he said. “It can be a combination of what we all want, and we could end up with great healthcare in our country. We could end up better than dealing with the Republicans.”

Despite touting his openness to work with Democrats, Trump has also repeatedly emphasized his power to veto legislation since Republican losses in the midterms.

“I’ll get along, probably, with the Democrats unless they want to be destructive,” Trump said the day after the election. “But I have the power of the veto.”

Trump did say in the interview with Fox News on Saturday that he does not think that vetoing “everything” passed by Democrats for the next two years is the way to go. But he also posted another image of himself on Truth Social later in the day, showing him in a red “VETO”-branded hat and a matching jacket.

In a statement Saturday afternoon, El-Sayed said he is “happy to chat” with the president if his intentions to work together on healthcare are genuine.

“If the President is serious about meeting the unmet promise of guaranteed healthcare in this country, I’m ready to work alongside leaders in the Senate like Senators Van Hollen, Sanders, Wyden, and Warren to deliver,” El-Sayed said. “President Trump, give me a call.”

data.title: Contenders to lead Senate Democrats reflect the party's split over Israel
data.description:
Race to lead Senate Democrats the latest battlefield in party’s tussle over Israel

Alice Speri
Sat, November 21, 2026 at 12:00 PM UTC
8 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The race to lead the Democratic Party's incoming Senate majority has become the latest battlefield between two conflicting visions for how the US should relate to Israel – a once unquestioned ally whose collapsing standing among the US public has become a defining feature of American politics.

Chuck Schumer, the veteran New York Senator and current Democratic minority leader, is one of Israel's most reliable supporters in Congress. As he views it, according to an interview he gave last year, his "job" is to "keep the left pro-Israel".

On the other side is Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland senator and challenger to Schumer for Senate leadership, who in recent years emerged as a steadfast advocate for Palestinian rights in the Senate. He supports sanctions, voted to block sales of weapons to Israel, and advocates for the families of US citizens killed by Israeli soldiers and settlers, as well as against the detention of Palestinian children by the Israeli military.

Advertisement

The two represent two opposing sides of the Democratic party's approach to Israel at a time when a majority of Democrats hold unfavorable views of it. Van Hollen has repeatedly visited the occupied West Bank. In January 2024 he traveled with Oregon's senator Jeff Merkley to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza, where they denounced Israel's restrictions on humanitarian aid.

While he has in recent years criticized Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and called him a "major obstacle" to peace, Schumer has been an unflinching supporter of Israel throughout his political career, repeatedly referring to himself as "Shomer Yisrael" or "guardian of Israel". Earlier this year, he said he views it as part of his job to fight for "all the aid that Israel needs".

He has opposed the Iran nuclear deal, the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, and a UN resolution affirming that Israeli settlements in occupied territory are illegal, and supported the US Embassy move to Jerusalem. During the war in Gaza, he has repeatedly voted against measures seeking to restrict military aid and weapons sales to Israel. He did, however, vote in favor of a failed resolution that would have required the state department to produce a report on Israeli human rights abuses in the West Bank, and has supported efforts to impose sanctions on individual settlers.

Schumer's office did not respond to a request for comment. In a statement, Van Hollen's office said that "the Israeli government has become increasingly hardline in its approach, diminishing the possibility of a two-state solution, including through its indiscriminate attacks on Gaza and its complicity in the escalating violence in the West Bank".

"The senator has urged the United States to use its leverage to push the government of Israel to comply with US policy and law."

While the Senate leader has ample discretion to set the party's legislative priorities and move bills to the floor for votes, he would not necessarily be able to influence the outcome of specific votes – or foreign policy – especially for the remainder of Trump's term.

Van Hollen has stressed that his challenge to Schumer is about delivering the "change from the status quo" that drove historic numbers of US voters to elect Democrats earlier this month. He has suggested he has the votes of 15 colleagues, but so far, only five have publicly pledged to back him including Michigan's newly elected Abdul El-Sayed, an outspoken critic of Israel, Merkley, Vermont's Bernie Sanders, Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan and Michigan's Elissa Slotkin. Several others have criticized Schumer and called for change but not committed to a vote.

While he is clearly the underdog in the race, Van Hollen insists he has a "path" to win. Whether or not he succeeds in his bid to oust Schumer, the race has significantly raised his national profile as an advocate for Palestinian rights.

Outside the Senate, advocacy groups' endorsements are largely following divides on Israel. Bend the Arc, a progressive Jewish group, noted that "the midterm elections proved that a majority of Americans are hungry for change and American Jews are no exception". The Institute for Middle Eastern Understanding's Policy Project cited Schumer's record as the only current Democratic senator to vote against the Iran nuclear deal as "paving the way" for the current war in Iran.

"Senator Van Hollen is committed to rights-respecting policy and understands that accountability is necessary to comprehensively challenge impunity," said Brad Parker, associate director of policy at the Center for Constitutional Rights.

"The recent electoral lesson over the past year is that incumbents who ignore the overwhelming and shifting electorate demands to end US complicity in Israeli crimes operate at their own peril."

Last week, dozens of protesters with the Sunrise Movement, a youth climate organization, were arrested outside Schumer's Washington office, where they called on the senator to "step up or step aside".

But Schumer – a titan of the party and the highest-ranking Jewish elected official in US history – has much of the political establishment behind him. He also has the backing of major pro-Israel groups.

"Jewish Americans have been a critical component of a winning Democratic coalition, including in the 2026 midterms," said Halie Soifer, the Jewish Democratic Council of America's CEO, which endorsed him. "We're confident that he'll lead Democrats to deliver for the American people in a way that is consistent with the values of the Jewish community in the 120th Congress."

On election night, before Van Hollen announced his challenge, Aipac also issued a statement congratulating Schumer and incoming House speaker Hakeem Jeffries for their caucuses' wins.

Despite significant shifts in rhetoric, Democratic officials have moved more slowly than their base. Earlier this year, 103 House Democrats voted to slash military aid to Israel – an unprecedented rebuke, but still less than half the party's caucus (only one Republican voted in favor). The Senate has been even more cautious.

While he has tried to focus on other issues since announcing his challenge, Van Hollen did reference his differences with Schumer on Israel – most notably when he accused him of having "joined with Aipac and crypto" to try to defeat Michigan's El-Sayed. Schumer favored El-Sayed's Aipac-backed opponent, Haley Stevens, during the primary, but he supported El-Sayed in the November general election. In an interview on Fox News on Sunday, Van Hollen spoke about growing settler violence in the West Bank, and the Israeli's government complicity in it. "I don't think American taxpayer dollars should be going to that purpose," he said.

"When I first spoke out about Gaza and what I thought – the bad conduct in Gaza – I was a pretty lonely voice, frankly," Van Hollen also said in an interview last year.

When he first ran for Senate a decade ago, Van Hollen was backed by some Aipac-aligned donors and regularly voted with most centrist Democrats on matters relating to Israel. But he has also had a longstanding interest in foreign policy, human rights, and the Middle East, and in his decade in the Senate he has frequently invoked the "Leahy law", which demands accountability for abuses by US-supported foreign militaries – including Israel's.

His criticism of Israel has grown more forceful over time. Following the 2022 West Bank killing of the Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, by an Israeli sniper, Van Hollen repeatedly met with her family and led the congressional response to the killing, aggressively pressing the Biden administration for accountability. (To this day, there has been none, and despite Van Hollen's repeated efforts, an official report on Abu Akleh's killing remains classified). Van Hollen's office said that Abu Akleh's killing "underscored for him the impunity with which the Israeli government was increasingly acting with regard to the West Bank".

In recent years, he has also championed the families of other US citizens killed by settlers and soldiers – including Rachel Corrie, Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, and Sayfollah Musallet. He also met with Mahmoud Khalil, the Columbia University student that has become the face of the Trump administration's crackdown on pro-Palestinian speech, shortly after Khalil was released from ICE detention. (When he was arrested, by contrast, Schumer issued a statement saying that he "abhor[s]" Khalil's views, though he added that if the Trump administration could not prove Khalil had committed a crime, his speech was protected by the US constitution.)

The contest is the latest proxy war over the future of the US-Israel relationship. It played an outsized role in mayoral elections in New York and Los Angeles, and defined heated Democratic primaries. It is dividing Republicans, and turning groups like Aipac into a liability for candidates.

Kidus Girma, campaign director for the Sunrise Movement, told the Guardian that while the speaker majority vote was about whether the Senate would respond to voters' calls for change from tackling climate action to getting money out of politics, support for Palestine had become "a litmus test issue for Democratic voters".

data.title: At least 11 people killed in Mexico's Sinaloa after capture of cartel boss, officials say
data.description:
11 killed in burst of violence in northern Mexico after capture of cartel leader

MEGAN JANETSKY, FABIOLA SÁNCHEZ and MARTÍN URISTA
Updated Sat, November 21, 2026 at 1:23 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Mexico Cartel Violence

1 of 6
This undated image released by the U.S. Department of State shows Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores. (U.S. Department of State via AP) (U.S. Department of State via AP)

GUASAVE, Mexico (AP) — A burst of violence in Mexico's Sinaloa state after authorities captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro," left at least 11 people dead, authorities said Saturday.

Meza Flores, one of the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after a heavy firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight left residents of the city of Guasave terrorized and trucks and businesses burning.

Mexico's Defense Cabinet on Saturday afternoon said that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed.

Advertisement

The capo climbed the cartel ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the leader of his own group, the Meza-Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. The United States had a $5 million reward offer for information leading to his arrest, and he was wanted for trafficking drugs to the U.S. and illegally carrying firearms.

Mexico's government said in a report early Saturday that intelligence from the Trump administration helped authorities capture him, but provided few details about how authorities in Mexico and the United States coordinated to detain Meza Flores.

He was also a key ally to "Los Mayos," a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was designated as a foreign terrorist organization by the Trump administration last year. His capture represents a blow to the cartel as it fights with another faction for control of the northern Mexican state.

Authorities in the United States and Mexico celebrated the arrest as a security win. U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Mexico's government to go after criminal groups.

As a fierce firefight settled into a tense calm Saturday, experts warned that picking off capos could set off another wave of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring cartel factions.

Mexican forces' move against cartel fuels violence

The capture of Meza Flores and his No. 2 in the city of Guasave, Sinaloa, set off a wave of violence when a firefight broke out around 7 p.m. on Friday, according to residents of the 290,000-person municipality. Soon, military helicopters and drones were flying overhead and opened fire on key locations across the city.

Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below. Such shows of force by cartels are common following the capture or killing of leaders.

"The fighting was happening all over Guasave," said Alma Camacho, a Guasave resident and local journalist. "It spread throughout the city."

Mexican authorities said that they used "stealth and surprise" to arrest Meza Flores, establishing a security perimeter around the building where he was located. After coming under attack with guns and explosives from suspected cartel operatives, armed forces personnel entered a home and detained him. He was later taken by aircraft to Mexico City to appear before prosecutors.

Video shared by authorities shows heavily armed men in camouflage escorting a man through a dimly lit house and putting him in the back of a truck. No casualties have been reported so far as a result of the operation.

Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4 a.m. on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he wasn't authorized to discuss the case.

"Getting him (Meza Flores) out was extraordinary," the official said, describing an intense response by members of the criminal group who maintained at least "10 roadblocks" with burning vehicles on Guasave's streets.

Terror in Sinaloa

Guasave resident and firefighter Paola Sánchez said that thousands of people were terrorized late Friday as they took shelter from intense gunfire in grocery stores and other locations.

"Last night, many businesses were burned ... along with cars and trucks," Sánchez told The Associated Press.

She said that the city's firefighters had to take shelter at their station and wait until Saturday morning for orders from their superiors to dispatch the first crews to check whether any businesses or vehicles were still burning.

An uneasy calm seemed to settle over the city Saturday. Mexican Security Secretary Omar García Harfuch wrote on X on Saturday morning that armed forces would remain deployed in Sinaloa state to protect civilians. Authorities didn't provide details on how many people were wounded or killed in the clashes.

Burned out trucks continued to line the freeway leading into the town, blocking roadways on Saturday.

"The aftermath of last night's war still lingers. Burned cars in the streets, several Oxxo stores completely burned down," Camacho said, referring to a chain of convenience stores in Mexico.

Guasave residents remained "very afraid" because security forces were absent from the streets, Camacho said.

Capture prompts celebration and warnings

Meza Flores' detention marks another high-profile capture of a cartel leader as Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum faces pressure from Trump to crack down on cartels. Sheinbaum has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors, and homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.

The U.S. and Mexican governments celebrated the capture on Saturday, with the DEA commending Mexican authorities.

"Results like these don't happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together," U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post. "We will continue the hunt."

Mexican Security Secretary García Harfuch called the detention "an important step in pacifying Sinaloa."

Sheinbaum's government has targeted a number of cartel kingpins, including Jalisco New Generation Cartel leader Nemesio Oseguera Cervantes, known as " El Mencho," who was killed by the military in February.

Mexican security analyst David Saucedo said that the capture of Meza Flores marked another case of the governments of Mexico and the U.S. increasingly falling back on a longstanding security strategy that critics warn could fuel more violence in the long run.

The so-called kingpin strategy relies on zeroing in on capos like Meza Flores as a way to combat cartels. But experts say that it often triggers violent power disputes among groups, like the one underway in Sinaloa.

"What is evident is this is a product of pressure from the United States," Saucedo said. "What they do is capture high-profile kingpins — the leaders — but they don't dismantle the entire organization. They arrested the No. 1 and No. 2, but the entire network of hit men, street-level drug dealers, businesses and political and police connections remains intact."

___

Megan Janetsky and Fabiola Sánchez reported from Mexico City. Thomas Strong contributed to this report from Washington.
